VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Acme Logistics
INDUSTRY: Logistics
COMPANY SIZE: 650 employees
STAGE: Discovery / first demo
DURATION: 30 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Rachel Morgan, VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics
- Tom Alvarez, Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics
TRANSCRIPT
[01:29] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): The short version is we've got too much operational work living between systems. And I want to be clear up front, we're not looking for another dashboard. We've got dashboards. We need something that actually moves work along and makes it visible who owns what.
[01:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can you give me a concrete one?
[01:51] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Sure. Handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success. All of that is managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders. So renewal risks and implementation blockers get noticed late. Not never — late.
[02:09] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How late is late?
[02:12] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Depends. Sometimes a week. Sometimes we find out at the QBR, which is — yeah.
[02:20] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And is it that the steps are manual, or —
[02:23] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): No, and this is the thing people get wrong. It's not that every step is manual. We have automation in places. The problem is the gaps between the automated pieces. Something runs, then nothing happens for four days, then a human notices.
[02:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the pattern we see most, actually. Connecting systems is one problem. Operating the process that sits on top of the connections is a different problem, and the second one is usually where the pain is.
[02:56] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Yeah.
[02:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you have numbers on it, or is it anecdotal?
[03:03] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Mix. We've got outcome metrics. The operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same thing happened fifteen times last month.
[03:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That last one is the one that costs you.
[03:27] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): That's the one that costs us, yes.
[03:32] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): — sorry, sorry, I'm here. Sorry. Was on with a customer.
[03:37] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No problem at all. We were just on current state.
[03:41] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Right. Well, my angle is slightly different from Rachel's. I want to make sure we don't buy a tool that looks great in a demo and then becomes another thing my team has to babysit. We've already got automation nobody quite owns.
[03:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Say more on that.
[04:00] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): When things work, nobody notices. When something sticks, the escalation path depends entirely on who happens to see it. And people compensate — they build their own reminders, their own little spreadsheets, someone wrote a script once. And then that person leaves.
[...]
[05:57] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can I correct something, actually — sorry, on the process thing. Earlier we described onboarding as standardised. That's what the deck says. In practice EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions. So a single workflow diagram on a slide is a bit misleading.
[...]
[06:21] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): The process people describe and the process people run are not always the same thing.
[...]
[08:19] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I'm more interested in a bounded set of workflows where the current approach is visibly failing.
[08:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Okay, so let me try one. If we picked a single workflow for phase one — opportunity closes in Salesforce, create the onboarding plan, assign tasks based on product mix, notify the right Slack channel, escalate stalled milestones up to CS leadership. Is that the right shape?
[...]
[09:00] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I want to see what happens when data's missing. When an API times out. When an approver does nothing for two days. When the account changes state halfway through the workflow.
[...]
[09:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's exactly the right level to test at, and it's the bit I'd want you to push on. Workflows are event-driven but each run holds state. So you can branch on data, pause for approvals, retry external actions, set timeout rules, and push an exception into a queue rather than just failing quietly.
[09:40] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can the queue be owned by a team? Not a named person. People change roles constantly here and individual ownership is genuinely one of the reasons our current stuff breaks.
[09:53] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And the run history persists, so an admin can see the inputs, which steps ran, where it stopped.
[...]
[10:12] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): There's a second use case I'd flag, not for phase one — identifying renewal risk by combining CRM fields, support activity and product usage signals out of Snowflake. I don't need it now. I do want to know the architecture doesn't rule it out.
[10:31] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It doesn't. Different shape of workflow — that's more scheduled and query-driven than event-driven — but same platform.
[...]
[11:18] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Right. So left-hand side is triggers and actions, middle is the flow, right-hand panel is the config for whatever step you've selected. A workflow can start from a SaaS event, a schedule, a webhook, a database query, or another workflow.
[...]
[12:12] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah, that's fair criticism and I'm not going to pretend. Simple mapping and branching is visual. Transformations use expressions. On Enterprise you can package reusable JavaScript steps if you need to. There's a generic REST action and webhooks. We don't claim every workflow is no-code. What we aim for is that the workflow stays understandable even if an engineer supplied one custom component.
[...]
[13:23] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I'd want that in the evaluation. A demo with clean data proves nothing to me.
[...]
[15:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You'd mentioned AI in your notes. I'll be brief on it because I don't think it's the centre of gravity here. We treat it as optional steps inside a workflow rather than making the whole product autonomous. Classification, summarisation, extracting fields from text, drafting something for a human to approve.
[...]
[15:43] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Rules for anything already structured and safety-critical. Model where the input is genuinely unstructured or the task is semantic. Summarising a long ticket thread, fine. Deciding whether to issue a refund above a threshold — that should stay deterministic and permissioned.
[16:03] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can we see the prompt and the model config? And can we switch AI off entirely for a workspace?
[...]
[16:44] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can the thing refuse to answer if the source material is thin? The failure mode I dislike is a very confident summary built on one incomplete note.
[16:56] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You can design for that. Require a minimum set of fields or sources before the AI step runs, ask the model to return structured confidence, route low-confidence cases to review. I wouldn't sell you model confidence as a mathematical guarantee though. The better control is usually evidence plus workflow policy.
[17:19] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): For anything customer-facing or exec-facing I'd want a link back to the underlying records. People need to be able to challenge the output.
[...]
[17:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Let me show you run history, actually, because it's related. [pause] So — filter by workflow, status, time, or a business field. Open a run, you get every step, inputs, outputs, timing, retries, any human approval.
[...]
[19:04] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Version history — if someone changes a condition on a Friday afternoon and it breaks, can we see exactly what changed?
[19:13] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Version history and change metadata, yes. Rollback and promotion patterns vary a bit by workflow and package. For your evaluation I'd actually suggest we include a change-management scenario rather than just building the thing once.
[...]
[19:40] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): It is, relatively. We need the usual vendor review, SSO, audit logs. We don't have a special data-residency requirement for this project.
[...]
[20:27] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Can you send the SOC 2 report, subprocessor list, DPA, architecture diagram, retention documentation?
[20:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes, all of that under the normal process, and we can complete your questionnaire. One ask from me — if anything on your list is an absolute gate, flag it now. I'd rather not spend six weeks on a pilot that can't pass review.
[...]
[23:18] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true. The stronger case is consistency and speed. We've got expensive people doing coordination work because the systems don't carry enough process context.
[23:38] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): And there's an engineering cost nobody sees. A script takes two days to write and then quietly eats a few hours every month forever. That never makes it into the original estimate.
[23:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For a pilot we can baseline one or two things before we automate — elapsed time, number of manual touches, exception rate, engineer hours spent maintaining the current process.
[24:06] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): I'd add adoption. A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation.
[24:15] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): And edge cases, not average time. The pain is always in the weird ten percent.
[...]
[24:47] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): With naming conventions. And change control on the important ones. And a rule that somebody other than the creator can understand each production flow.
[...]
[26:17] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Fair enough. Look — my read is I'm interested enough to test it. If you can give us a sandbox I can supply three real workflows and we'll see whether the exception handling is as good as it looked today.
[26:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's exactly what I'd want. So — we send the security pack and a short architecture summary, you send the representative workflow and sample data, and we jointly write three to five pilot success criteria. Then we decide on the sandbox.
[...]
[27:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Can a human modify data before approving? Sometimes approval isn't just yes or no.
[27:38] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Approval forms can collect structured inputs and those values feed subsequent steps. For heavily customised forms some customers use their own front end and call us through the API.
[27:52] Tom Alvarez (Director of Customer Success, Acme Logistics): Last one. Can we trigger a workflow manually for a one-off exception?
[27:58] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes, permissions allowing. It's useful during migration and for exception recovery.
[...]
[28:31] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): Yes. And keep the first workflow narrow. I'd rather have one thing we trust than six demos.

The clearest purchase signals are in CALL-013, CALL-009, CALL-005, CALL-001, and CALL-004: each has an explicit next step plus a real business case, and several name a near-term timeline or decision gate. CALL-002, CALL-008, CALL-010, CALL-007, CALL-006, and CALL-016 look more conditional because they have interest but also hard blockers or early-stage hesitation; CALL-017, CALL-018, CALL-019, and CALL-020 look much less likely near term because they are either cold outreach or explicitly not ready.

CALL ID: CALL-011
DATE: 2026-09-02
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
CUSTOMER: Lumen Retail Group
INDUSTRY: Grocery retail
COMPANY SIZE: 3,200 employees
STAGE: Renewal / QBR
DURATION: 21 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Fiona Bright, Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group
- Devan Shah, Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group
TRANSCRIPT
[00:23] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Right. Let me start with numbers and then you tell me what I've missed. You're fourteen months in. Twenty-two workflows in production, up from six at the end of the first quarter. Run volume's roughly two hundred and eighty thousand a month.
[...]
[00:43] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Error rate's sitting at one point four percent, which is down from four point one when you started. Most of that improvement came in April.
[00:53] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): April was when we fixed the store-data validation. That was our fault, not yours.
[...]
[01:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Yes. Median time from exception raised to first action is now forty minutes. It was — Devan, what was it before?
[01:20] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Between two and six hours, depending on who was on.
[...]
[01:31] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): That's the one that's changed how the depots work. Genuinely. I had a depot manager tell me in July that he'd stopped keeping his own spreadsheet, and that's — you don't get that often.
[...]
[02:03] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Overages. You've exceeded your contracted run volume in four of the last six months. June was twenty-two percent over.
[...]
[02:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You were charged for two of them. Two were waived — one in March because it was a retry storm caused by a Salesforce outage on their side, and one in May which I waived because you'd flagged it to us proactively before the invoice.
[...]
[02:51] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Appreciated. But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
[...]
[03:08] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): The retry storm in March. Has anything changed at your end so that doesn't happen again? Because from our side we did nothing wrong and it cost us twenty thousand runs.
[03:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Partly. There are retry controls and you can set caps per workflow, and we can look at whether yours are configured sensibly — I suspect two or three of them aren't. But if a downstream system is down for six hours and your workflows keep firing, you will burn runs.
[...]
[04:04] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Yes. I'll put an hour in with Devan for the fortnight after next.
[...]
[04:23] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Two of those have moved teams.
[...]
[04:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I have exactly the same view. Nine licensed builders with four dormant is a renewal that gets scrutinised. I'd rather sell you seven active seats and a higher run tier than nine seats where four are indefensible.
[...]
[05:06] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Braced for "here's a fifteen percent uplift, sign here."
[...]
[05:37] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): So — at the moment, bringing on a new supplier involves about nine handoffs between buying, compliance, finance and the depot systems team. It's email and a SharePoint list.
[...]
[05:54] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Target's fifteen working days. Actual is somewhere around thirty.
[05:59] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Thirty-four last quarter.
[...]
[06:21] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): It's both, but I'd say the reason it's an organisational problem is that nobody can see where it's stuck. If you could see it, the arguing would stop.
[06:33] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's usually true. I'd flag one risk though — if the process itself is genuinely broken, automating it makes it a faster broken process.
[...]
[06:52] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then I'd suggest the first phase is visibility only. Don't automate the handoffs. Just instrument them — track where a supplier onboarding is, who has it, how long they've had it. Run that for six weeks and look at the data.
[...]
[07:31] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): [pause] Yes. Let's do that.
[...]
[08:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): List uplift at renewal is seven percent. That's the standard annual adjustment and I'm not going to pretend it's negotiable in principle — it applies to everyone.
[...]
[08:44] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): But the run tier change is a bigger number than the uplift, and I want to be upfront about that. You need three hundred and fifty thousand, not two fifty, and that's before the supplier onboarding work.
[...]
[09:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Three fifty gives you about twenty percent headroom on your current trajectory. Four hundred gives you a year and the instrumentation project.
[...]
[09:16] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll send exact numbers, but roughly — the step from two fifty to three fifty is the significant one. Three fifty to four hundred is a smaller increment because of how the tiers are shaped.
[...]
[09:46] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Directionally, with seven seats instead of nine, seven percent uplift, and the four hundred thousand tier — you're looking at roughly nine percent above what you paid this year. If we kept nine seats it'd be closer to fourteen.
[10:04] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): [pause] Nine percent for forty percent more capacity and a new use case.
[10:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the shape of it. And I want to be clear that the seat reduction is genuine — I'm not inflating the run tier to compensate.
[...]
[10:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): There is. A two-year commitment lets me fix the uplift for year two, which given where inflation's gone is probably worth more than the discount itself.
[...]
[11:25] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Because you're fourteen months into a platform that's going well, and three years is a long commitment for something you haven't yet used for the harder use case. If supplier onboarding goes badly you'd be locked into a tier you don't need. Two years is where I'd sit.
[...]
[11:56] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Alright. Model two years, and model three so I can see it, and I'll decide.
[...]
[12:17] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Response times have been fine. Resolution times on anything involving the SAP connector have been terrible. We had a ticket open for nineteen days in July.
[...]
[12:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It sat for eleven days and there's no good explanation. I've raised it internally and the honest answer I got was that it fell between two teams.
[...]
[12:56] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What I can do is name a specific engineer as the escalation contact for SAP issues on your account. What I can't do is promise you a resolution SLA on connector defects, because we don't offer one and I'm not going to invent it at a renewal.
[...]
[13:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Your Enterprise agreement already includes priority support with response-time commitments. Resolution-time commitments are a different thing and we don't do them. If someone tells you otherwise, check the paper.
[...]
[13:50] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): You've got twenty-two production workflows and your naming convention has drifted. There are four called some variant of "depot exception" and I genuinely could not tell you which is live.
[...]
[17:32] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's clause fourteen. It went in at the original signature because your legal team asked for it.
[...]
[17:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Nothing binding. What you'll get from me by Friday is the renewal proposal with last year's line items next to next year's, seven seats, four hundred thousand runs, and one-year, two-year and three-year options priced separately.
[...]
[18:06] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The seat reduction is in there and it's called out explicitly so your finance director can see it.
[...]
[18:15] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): From me — the retry configuration session with Devan, the subprocessor list for Priyanka, a short note on what the supplier onboarding instrumentation phase would look like, and the named SAP escalation contact.
[...]
[19:39] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): [pause] The depot exception routing. Without question. Everything else we could go back to doing the old way and survive. That one has changed the operating rhythm and going back would be genuinely painful.
[...]
[20:04] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Because when something breaks I can answer the question in four minutes instead of half a day. That's not visible to Fiona but it's most of my quality of life.

=== CALL-012 (call kind: renewal)
CALL ID: CALL-012
DATE: 2026-09-08
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
CUSTOMER: Pinewood Insurance
INDUSTRY: Insurance
COMPANY SIZE: 1,400 employees
STAGE: Renewal / at risk
DURATION: 23 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Graham Attwood, Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance
- Nadia Rahman, IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Morning Graham, morning Nadia. Thanks for making the time — I know this one's been rescheduled twice.
[00:08] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Three times, I think. That's on us.
[00:12] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I wasn't counting.
[00:14] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): You were, but that's fine.
[00:17] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Slightly. Look, I want to be direct about why I asked for this. Your renewal's on the twenty-ninth of November. Usage has dropped about forty percent since March. And I've had two conversations with Nadia that suggested you're not happy. I'd rather have the awkward conversation now than a surprise in November.
[00:41] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): That's fair.
[00:43] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): It's also accurate.
[00:46] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then tell me. Start wherever you want.
[00:50] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): The honest answer is that I inherited this. Ravi bought it, Ravi implemented it, Ravi left in February, and I picked it up in March with about forty minutes of handover.
[01:05] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Forty minutes.
[01:07] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Forty minutes and a Confluence page that was last edited in November.
[01:13] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): The Confluence page is quite good, in fairness.
[01:17] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): The Confluence page is the only reason anything still works.
[01:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a failure on our side too. When your named champion leaves, we should be re-onboarding whoever picks it up, and nobody did that.
[01:33] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): No, nobody did.
[01:35] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I took over your account in May. It should have been the first thing I did and it wasn't.
[01:42] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] I appreciate you saying that rather than telling me about a training portal.
[01:49] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): There is a training portal.
[01:51] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): I know there is. I've never opened it.
[01:54] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Nobody opens it.
[01:56] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): [laughs]
[01:58] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Let me put the numbers up and you tell me what they mean from where you sit. You've got fourteen workflows in production. Six of them haven't run successfully in the last ninety days.
[02:12] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Which six?
[02:14] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'll send the list, but broadly — three are the claims triage set, two are broker onboarding, and one is something called "TEMP - do not use" which has been running on a schedule since January.
[02:29] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] It's been running since January?
[02:33] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It's been failing since January. Every four hours.
[02:38] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Nobody told us.
[02:40] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): You'd have got the failure alerts. They're going to Ravi's address, which still exists as a shared mailbox that nobody reads.
[02:50] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Oh, for goodness' sake.
[02:53] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): That's — yeah. That's on us.
[02:56] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It's on both of us. You should have redirected the alerts. We should have noticed a workflow failing two thousand times and rung someone.
[03:07] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Do you not monitor that?
[03:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Not proactively at your account tier, no. And I'd rather tell you that plainly than imply we're watching when we aren't.
[03:20] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] Right.
[03:22] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Is that something you do at a higher tier?
[03:26] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): There's more proactive review on the largest accounts. It's not a product feature you can buy, it's how our team allocates time, and I don't want to dress that up as something it isn't.
[03:40] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): I'd rather know.
[03:42] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): The three claims triage ones concern me more than the temp one. Those were the reason you bought.
[03:50] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): They were the reason Ravi bought.
[03:53] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Are they still the reason?
[03:56] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] I don't know. That's the honest answer. The claims director changed in April and the new one has a different view about where triage should happen.
[04:09] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): She wants it in Guidewire.
[04:12] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Ah.
[04:14] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): She wants it in Guidewire, and she has a point, because that's where the claims handlers already are.
[04:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a legitimate architectural position and I'm not going to argue against it. Can Guidewire do the cross-system part? The bit that pulls from the broker portal and the document store?
[04:36] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Not natively. That's what we'd have to build.
[04:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): With what?
[04:43] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Power Automate, probably. Or Guidewire's own integration layer, which our vendor tells us is capable and our developers tell me is painful.
[04:55] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Which do you believe?
[04:58] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): [laughs] The developers. Always the developers.
[05:03] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): So the situation is that half of what we bought this for might move somewhere else, and the other half — broker onboarding — is stalled for a completely different reason.
[05:16] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Which is?
[05:18] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Nobody's building anything. We've got four builder licences. One person uses it. She's brilliant, she's called Ellie, and she's been on maternity leave since June.
[05:32] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So you have a bus factor of one and the bus arrived.
[05:37] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): The bus arrived, yes.
[05:40] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): We tried to get two people up to speed in July. It didn't take.
[05:46] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Why not?
[05:48] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): They're busy. And the learning curve for the first workflow is steeper than the marketing suggests.
[05:56] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): How steep?
[05:58] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): One of them spent two days on it and produced something that didn't work, and then went back to their actual job. Which I entirely understand.
[06:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Did they ask for help?
[06:12] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): No.
[06:14] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Would they have known who to ask?
[06:17] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] Probably not.
[06:20] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's the bit I can actually fix.
[06:23] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Can you?
[06:25] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Some of it. Enablement sessions, office hours, a named contact. What I can't fix is that your people are busy and this isn't their day job. If the only person who ever built anything was Ellie, then when Ellie's not here you have a very expensive product that nobody operates.
[06:47] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): That's precisely the position I'm in.
[06:51] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I come in?
[06:53] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Please.
[06:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've been listening and I want to say something that probably isn't in my interest. You're on Enterprise. Looking at what you're actually using, I'm not sure you should be.

[11:11] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then take the export. It's better to have it and not need it.

[11:31] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Everyone does. And I'll arrange a deletion confirmation for afterwards with an actual date on it.
[11:39] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Thank you.
[11:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Your contract ends the eleventh of November. Do you want read-only access past that?
[11:47] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Two weeks would help. We'll be running both in parallel through October.

[11:58] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): That's generous.

[12:03] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [laughs] Some vendors are petty.
[12:07] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Some vendors are very petty.

[12:22] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] With the approval forms, yes. Without them, no, because that's the bit Zapier can't do and it's the only thing I'll actually miss.
[12:34] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So approval forms are the feature.

[12:47] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's genuinely useful and I'll pass it on.

answer.summary: The customers who left mostly did so because the product did not fit how they actually used it: Pinewood was paying for Enterprise but getting little active use, with a key question of whether the workflow role and enablement existed at all; Verity concluded it had bought an engineering tool rather than a business-user tool; and Oakhill found it was on a plan far larger than its needs. In all three cases, pricing mattered, but it was secondary to poor fit, low adoption, or missing capabilities. There was also a recurring complaint that proper enablement or the right smaller package was absent.

claims.statement: Pinewood Insurance left because the product was delivering very little for what they were paying, and their renewal question became whether Enterprise was worth it at all.

citations.speaker: Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
citations.quote: the honest answer is probably not, because you're getting very little.

citations.speaker: Nadia Rahman, IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance
citations.quote: I don't think the product is the problem. I think we implemented it badly

claims.statement: Pinewood's deeper issue was that only one person could build workflows, so when she left or went on leave, nobody else could operate the product.

citations.speaker: Graham Attwood, Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance
citations.quote: We've got four builder licences. One person uses it.

citations.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
citations.quote: when Ellie's not here you have a very expensive product that nobody operates.

claims.statement: Pinewood also had a business-process disagreement about moving claims triage to Guidewire, which reduced the case for continuing OrbitFlow on that use case.

citations.speaker: Graham Attwood, Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance
citations.quote: she has a point, because that's where the claims handlers already are.

citations.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
citations.quote: if claims triage is moving, then the case for this product rests entirely on broker onboarding

claims.statement: Pinewood's agreement also had a short auto-renew notice window, and the team did not know about it until the call, which affected their exit planning but was not the reason for leaving.

citations.speaker: Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
citations.quote: Your current contract auto-renews with sixty days' notice

citations.speaker: Graham Attwood, Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance
citations.quote: So I need to serve notice by the thirtieth regardless, to keep my options open.

claims.statement: Verity Payments left because it had to build custom integrations anyway, so the platform's main promise was not being realized.

citations.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist, Engineering Manager, Verity Payments
citations.quote: we ended up writing a custom integration either way

citations.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist, Engineering Manager, Verity Payments
citations.quote: maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations.

claims.statement: Verity's operations team never built the workflows, so the company ended up using OrbitFlow as an engineering tool rather than a business-user tool.

citations.speaker: Kwame Boateng, Head of Operations, Verity Payments
citations.quote: Nobody in operations ever built anything.

citations.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist, Engineering Manager, Verity Payments
citations.quote: We've bought an engineering tool and stopped pretending.

claims.statement: Verity said the connector gap was real, but its head of operations said that was not the real reason for leaving.

citations.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist, Engineering Manager, Verity Payments
citations.quote: You don't have a connector for them.

citations.speaker: Kwame Boateng, Head of Operations, Verity Payments
citations.quote: The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left.

claims.statement: Oakhill Property left because it was on a much larger and more expensive plan than it needed for its simple automation use case.

citations.speaker: Hazel Wren, Operations Director, Oakhill Property
citations.quote: We bought something we didn't need.

citations.speaker: Hazel Wren, Operations Director, Oakhill Property
citations.quote: We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in.

claims.statement: Oakhill said the product worked, but the value was not worth the annual cost for a company its size.

citations.speaker: Hazel Wren, Operations Director, Oakhill Property
citations.quote: They worked perfectly. That's the frustrating part.

citations.speaker: Hazel Wren, Operations Director, Oakhill Property
citations.quote: They're worth something. They're not worth nineteen thousand pounds a year to a company our size.

claims.statement: Oakhill also wanted a smaller, cheaper plan and said that if such a plan had existed, it likely would have stayed.

citations.speaker: Hazel Wren, Operations Director, Oakhill Property
citations.quote: There should be a smaller plan.

citations.speaker: Hazel Wren, Operations Director, Oakhill Property
citations.quote: If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer

conflicts.description: Pinewood's main reason for leaving was presented two ways: account-underuse / poor fit vs implementation failure. Nadia says the product was not the problem and that they implemented it badly; Leo/Ruth say the account got very little value and the product depended on a role they did not have.

citations.speaker: Nadia Rahman, IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance
citations.quote: I don't think the product is the problem. I think we implemented it badly

citations.speaker: Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
citations.quote: the honest answer is probably not, because you're getting very little.

citations.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
citations.quote: you have a very expensive product that nobody operates.

conflicts.why: More specific about the mechanism, repeated by multiple speakers across the call, and tied to the missing builder role and enablement; the 'product is not the problem' view is a customer opinion rather than a full explanation.

conflicts.description: Verity's departure was framed as connector-gap driven by Sarah, but Kwame corrected that it was not the real reason, only a symptom.

conflicts.better_supported: connector gap was only a symptom
conflicts.why: Kwame explicitly corrects the earlier framing and explains the real reason as lack of operational builders and the platform being used as an engineering tool.

conflicts.description: Oakhill's reason for leaving was price/plan mismatch versus product fit. Hazel says the product worked and the issue was paying too much for more capacity than needed, while also saying the smaller plan would have kept her.

conflicts.why: The transcript repeatedly ties the exit to overbuying and missing a smaller plan, while praising the product itself and saying the workflows worked perfectly.

not_found: The transcripts do not support a single universal reason across all churned customers; each call gives a different mix of price, fit, capability, and adoption issues.

They do not show any of the shown customers leaving because OrbitFlow 'didn't work' in a simple product-failure sense; in the departing calls, the product is usually described as working or partly working.
answer.confidence_reason: The three shown churn calls directly explain why each customer left, with multiple customer-side admissions and vendor summaries. The evidence is explicit enough to distinguish primary reasons from side issues like notice windows or support complaints.

[25:29] Rachel Morgan (VP Revenue Operations, Acme Logistics): One representative workflow working with real enough data. Security gates understood. answer.summary: Renewals are handled much more like an account-management and commercial-renewal process: a CSM often leads, the team uses the existing contract as the baseline, and they discuss line items, seat counts, renewal timing, and even bridge or shorter-term options. New business calls are more exploratory: AEs and solutions engineers jointly diagnose the workflow, run the discovery/demo, and set up pilots or proof-of-concepts with concrete success criteria and sample data rather than talking renewal terms.

[00:50] Chloe Barnes (Executive Assistant, Silverline Travel): [pause] She's the right person. She's also very busy this week — we've got a supplier conference.
[00:58] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then I don't want to interrupt her. Would it be better if I called back next week?
[01:05] Chloe Barnes (Executive Assistant, Silverline Travel): Honestly? Probably. Thursday or Friday.

[01:14] Chloe Barnes (Executive Assistant, Silverline Travel): Go on.

[04:34] Martine Duval (Director of Customer Operations, Silverline Travel): That is — yes. That's accurate.
[04:38] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is it a problem for you, or is it handled?

[05:28] Martine Duval (Director of Customer Operations, Silverline Travel): Send me the page and copy Chloe. If the page is good she'll put it in the diary.
[05:35] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood. Thank you for the five minutes.
[05:39] Martine Duval (Director of Customer Operations, Silverline Travel): Three.
[05:41] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Three. Goodbye.

There is also an inconsistency in how the product is described on code requirements: one rep called it “completely no-code,” while others said OrbitFlow does not claim every workflow is no-code and that custom components can require JavaScript or other code. Overall, the Enterprise-only SSO answer is better supported.

question: How many Zapier automations does Cedar & Finch run, and how many of them touch Zendesk?

context.text:
=== CALL-003 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-003
DATE: 2026-06-11
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Cedar & Finch
INDUSTRY: E-commerce
COMPANY SIZE: 180 employees
STAGE: Discovery / demo
DURATION: 17 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Leo Grant, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Sophie Reed, Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch
- Marcus Lee, Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Hi both. Sophie, Marcus — thanks for making time.
[00:04] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Hi. Marcus is on his phone, he's between things.
[00:09] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Yeah, sorry, I'm walking. I'll be at a desk in five.
[00:14] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No problem. So normally I'd spend twenty minutes on discovery before showing anything, but —
[00:21] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Can we not?
[00:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Go on.
[00:25] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): We've done three of these in a fortnight. I can recite our own pain points. Can we just see it and I'll interrupt when something matters?
[00:35] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Deal. I'll ask about four questions along the way rather than up front. Fair?
[00:41] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Fair.
[00:43] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): One thing before I share — I'm on my own today. Nina, our solutions engineer, is with another customer. So if you ask me something properly technical I'm going to say "I'll come back to you" rather than make it up.
[00:58] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): I'd prefer that, honestly.
[01:02] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right. Sharing. [pause] Can you see it?
[01:07] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Yep.
[01:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So this is the workflow builder. Triggers and actions on the left, the flow in the middle, and whatever step you've clicked gets its config on the right.
[01:20] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've pre-built something that I think is roughly your world. High-value order comes in, there's a fulfilment exception on it, we open a ticket, we ping a channel, we update a tracker.
[01:34] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): That's — yeah, that's almost exactly it. Detect high-value orders with fulfilment exceptions, Zendesk ticket, right Slack channel, and update our Airtable exception tracker.
[01:48] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let me just run it. [pause] So it's triggered off the order event, it checks the value threshold, it checks the exception flag, and then it branches.
[02:01] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Stop there. What happens if the order data's incomplete?
[02:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Good. So — this branch here. If the required fields aren't populated it doesn't just carry on, it drops into an exception queue.
[02:17] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Owned by who?
[02:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): A team, not a person. You can route to a group, or resolve a person dynamically off a field, or use an on-call style fallback.
[02:29] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Okay. That's relevant, because — Marcus, are you back?
[02:34] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): I'm here, I'm sitting down.
[02:37] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Tell him the number.
[02:39] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Right, so. We've got more than sixty Zapier automations. Six-zero. And several of them are owned by people who don't work here any more.
[02:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How do you find out when one breaks?
[02:53] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): When a customer complains.
[02:56] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] Right.
[02:59] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): That's not a joke, that's genuinely the detection mechanism.
[03:04] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): It's the honest answer.
[03:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's a very common answer. It's just usually not said out loud in the first ten minutes.
[03:14] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Well, we're not going to fix it by pretending.
[03:18] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No. Okay, so let me show you the bit that speaks to that. [pause] This is run history. Filter by workflow, status, time. Open any run and you see every step, the inputs, the outputs, timings, retries.
[03:36] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Can I set an alert on a failure rate rather than an individual failure? Because sixty automations, if I get an email per failure I'll just filter them into a folder and never look at it.
[03:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes — you can alert when error rates cross a threshold. And that's the right instinct, everyone who alerts per-failure ends up ignoring all of them.
[04:01] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Learned that one the hard way.
[04:05] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Can I correct something Sophie said in the email, actually?
[04:09] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Go on.
[04:11] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): I think I may have overstated the Zendesk angle earlier. Support feels like the loudest problem because failures surface there — that's where the customer shouts. But honestly, probably only about a quarter of the automations actually touch Zendesk.
[04:31] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a really useful correction. What do the other three quarters touch?
[04:37] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Shopify mostly. Klaviyo. Some Airtable stuff.
[04:42] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Let me give you the full list. Shopify, Zendesk, Klaviyo, Slack, Airtable, and Zapier holding it all together with string.
[04:53] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And of those, which one is the one that has to work perfectly?
[04:58] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Shopify. A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
[05:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood. I'm going to be careful here — I believe the Shopify integration is native and event-driven, but I'm not going to swear to the exact trigger coverage without checking. That's a Nina question and I'll get you a written answer.
[05:24] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Fine.
[05:26] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What about volume? Roughly.
[05:29] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Off peak, about eight thousand orders a week. Peak is — Marcus?
[05:35] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Peak is silly. Three, four times that in the run-up to Christmas.
[05:41] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And you're UK and EU?
[05:43] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): UK and EU, yes. Which is a security question, so let me do that bit now while I remember.
[05:51] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go for it.
[05:53] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): We need a standard DPA. SSO would be nice rather than mandatory — we're a hundred and eighty people, I'm not going to pretend we've got a zero-trust programme. And because we sell into the UK and EU I want to understand where customer data actually gets processed.
[06:14] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That last one I can answer partly. EU data residency is available on Enterprise. On Growth, I'd need to confirm the default processing region for you in writing rather than guess.
[06:28] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Enterprise. That's the expensive one.
[06:31] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the expensive one, yes.
[06:34] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Then let's do money now, because I don't want to spend twenty minutes falling in love with this.
[06:41] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Sensible. Growth starts at eighteen hundred a month, up to thirty users, on an annual agreement.
[06:49] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): [pause] Right.
[06:52] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Say it.
[06:54] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
[07:04] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a real gap. I'm not going to pretend it isn't.
[07:09] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): I could potentially do an annual prepay if that materially changes the number. Does it?
[07:16] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It can. I'd be lying if I said it halves it. It's a meaningful discount, not a transformation.
[07:24] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Mm.
[07:26] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): What's the Zapier bill at the moment, Soph?
[07:30] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Ours? About two hundred and something. But that's not the comparison and you know it, because the two hundred doesn't include the four hours a week you spend chasing broken ones.
[07:43] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): It's more than four.
[07:45] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): [crosstalk] I know it's more than four. I'm being generous to my own argument.
[07:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That is actually the argument, though. Can I ask — if you priced Marcus's time and the customer complaints, what does the current setup cost you?
[08:01] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): I genuinely don't know. Nobody's ever asked me to count it.
[08:07] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): And that's the problem with building the business case. I can't put "vibes" in a spreadsheet for the finance director.
[08:15] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No. But you could count it for four weeks before you decide anything. That's free and it'd make the conversation much easier either way.
[08:26] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): That's — yeah. That's a fair suggestion.
[08:31] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): I can log it. It'll be depressing but I can log it.
[08:36] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let me show you two more things and then I'll stop. [pause] This is the templates and reusable components bit. Rather than sixty separate automations, you'd typically build a handful of subflows — order lookup, notification, ticket creation — and assemble from those.
[08:57] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): So when something changes I change it in one place.
[09:02] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): In one place, yes. And that's genuinely the thing I'd point at for your sixty-Zap problem. It's not that we do things Zapier can't. It's that sixty independent Zaps is sixty things to maintain and this is more like eight.
[09:20] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Okay. That is the most compelling thing you've said.
[09:25] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll take it.
[09:27] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): What about visibility of who owns what? Because the dead-employee problem is real.
[09:34] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Version history and change metadata on every workflow. So you can see what changed and when. And you'd typically define who can publish to production versus who can build in a dev workspace.
[09:49] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): We don't have a dev workspace. We don't have a dev anything.
[09:54] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] You'd get one. That's not extra cost, it's just how it's structured.
[10:00] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Do you do the AI stuff? Everyone does the AI stuff now.
[10:05] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): We do, but I'd underplay it for you. It's optional steps inside a workflow — classification, summarisation, extracting fields out of text, drafting something a human then approves. It's not an autonomous agent thing.
[10:22] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Is there something there for us or are you being polite?
[10:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): There might be one. You mentioned wanting a weekly digest of recurring support reasons pushed to the e-commerce and product teams?
[10:37] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): That was me. I want that. I've wanted that for two years.
[10:42] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a reasonable fit — summarise the week's tickets by theme, with links back to the underlying tickets so someone can check it.
[10:52] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): With links. Because I don't trust a summary I can't verify.
[10:57] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You shouldn't. And that's how we'd build it — the source references stored next to the generated output.
[11:05] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Does that cost extra?
[11:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connectors. I'd want to model that for your volumes rather than say "no" and surprise you later.
[11:19] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.
[11:23] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let me put the assumptions in writing and you can hold me to them.
[11:29] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Okay.
[11:32] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask about decision-making? If you did want to do this, what's the path?
[11:38] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): I can choose tools under fifteen thousand a year on my own. Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
[11:47] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And eighteen hundred a month is —
[11:50] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Twenty-one, six. So it goes upstairs. Which is a different conversation and a slower one.
[11:58] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood. That's useful to know now rather than in six weeks.
[12:04] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): I'm telling you because I'd rather not waste either of our time.
[12:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Appreciated. Timing?
[12:12] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): I'd like to clean up the automations before the holiday peak. Ideally something in place by early October, because after that nobody's changing anything until January.
[12:25] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Nobody touches anything in November. Company rule.
[12:29] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Sensible rule. So realistically a decision in — August?
[12:35] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): August, if we do it.
[12:38] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right. Let me ask the uncomfortable one. What's the alternative? Not "do nothing" — the real alternative.
[12:47] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Honestly? Zapier and Make. I like Zapier for the simple stuff, it does what it says. And I've tested Make for the more complicated branching, which it handles better than I expected.
[13:03] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And the concern with those?
[13:06] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Maintenance and visibility. The same two things. Make would give me the branching but I'd still have the ownership problem.
[13:16] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): And nobody here knows Make except Sophie.
[13:20] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Which is its own ownership problem.
[13:24] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So the honest framing is: we'd have to beat Zapier plus better documentation and ownership discipline. Not beat doing nothing.
[13:35] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): That's exactly right. And to be blunt — budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership. That's a real outcome and it might be the right one.
[13:53] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It might be. I'd rather you concluded that in July than in month five.
[14:00] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): You keep saying things that don't sound like sales.
[14:04] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've been doing this a while. The deals that go wrong are the ones where someone talked themselves past a genuine objection.
[14:13] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Mm.
[14:16] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Sorry — Soph, you've frozen.
[14:19] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): [inaudible]
[14:21] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): You're breaking up. Leo, can you hear her?
[14:25] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Not really.
[14:27] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): — sorry. Sorry. Back. My office wifi is genuinely worse than my house wifi and I don't understand why.
[14:36] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Mine too. Where'd we lose you?
[14:40] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): You were being honest about objections, which I appreciated, and then I vanished, which was poor timing.
[14:48] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So — where does that leave you? Genuinely.
[14:53] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): I like the monitoring. I like the reusable templates. That's the bit that speaks to our actual problem. I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
[15:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a completely fair position.
[15:13] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): I'm not saying no.
[15:16] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I know. And I'd rather have a considered maybe than an enthusiastic yes that dies in procurement.
[15:24] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): What would you want from us?
[15:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Two things, and both are cheap. One — Marcus logs the time spent on broken automations for four weeks. Not for me, for you. Two — send me your three worst automations, the ones that break most, and I'll come back with what they'd look like rebuilt here, plus an honest note on which bits are actually better and which are just different.
[15:53] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): You'll tell me which bits aren't better?
[15:56] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): If I don't, you'll find out in month two and then I've lost you anyway.
[16:02] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Alright. Marcus, can you do the logging thing?
[16:06] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): I can do the logging thing.
[16:09] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Then yes. Send me that.
[16:12] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll also get you written answers on the Shopify trigger coverage and the default processing region. Those are the two I dodged.
[16:22] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): You did dodge them.
[16:24] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Deliberately.
[16:26] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Better than the alternative.
[16:29] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Anything else before we drop?
[16:32] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Actually, yeah, one. If we did buy this, do we have to migrate all sixty at once?
[16:39] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): God, no. Please don't. The pattern that works is picking the three that break most, moving those, running both for a bit, then deciding. Big-bang migrations of sixty automations is how these projects die.
[16:56] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): Okay. That's reassuring.
[17:00] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): Right. I've got another one at half past. Thanks, Leo.
[17:05] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks both. And Marcus — sorry about the logging homework.
[17:11] Marcus Lee (Customer Support Manager, Cedar & Finch): [laughs] It's fine. It'll be useful either way.
[17:16] Sophie Reed (Director of E-commerce Operations, Cedar & Finch): That's the spirit. Bye.
[17:19] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Bye.

[02:37] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): I didn't know that.
[02:39] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): I knew about March. I didn't know about May.

[02:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The run tier is wrong, yes. Which is most of what I want to talk about.

[08:39] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Seven.

[04:58] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): [laughs] The developers. Always the developers.

[05:32] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So you have a bus factor of one and the bus arrived.

[05:40] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): We tried to get two people up to speed in July. It didn't take.

[05:48] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): They're busy. And the learning curve for the first workflow is steeper than the marketing suggests.

[05:58] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): One of them spent two days on it and produced something that didn't work, and then went back to their actual job. Which I entirely understand.
[06:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Did they ask for help?

[06:17] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] Probably not.

[06:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've been listening and I want to say something that probably isn't in my interest. You're on Enterprise. Looking at what you're actually using, I'm not sure you should be.

[07:27] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): SSO, obviously. Audit export — no. Residency — we're UK only and we're on the EU region, so, technically yes, but it's not a requirement anyone's written down.
[07:41] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Advanced workspace governance?
[07:44] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): We have one workspace.
[07:46] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right.
[07:48] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): What's the alternative?
[07:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Growth. Eighteen hundred a month, up to thirty users, annual. You'd lose SCIM, audit export, EU residency as a contractual commitment, some of the governance controls, and priority support drops to standard.
[08:07] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): We'd lose SSO?
[08:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): SAML SSO is Enterprise. So yes, that's the one that would actually hurt.
[08:16] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): That's a problem. Our security standard requires SSO for anything holding claims data.
[08:24] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then Growth isn't viable and I've just talked myself out of my own suggestion.
[08:30] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [laughs] That was quick.
[08:33] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's better to find out now. But it does mean the question is different — it's not "which tier", it's "is Enterprise worth it for what you're getting", and right now the honest answer is probably not, because you're getting very little.
[08:50] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): So what do you suggest?

[09:09] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): You're offering me that?
[09:11] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather offer it than have you sign a renewal you resent and churn next year with a bad taste.
[09:19] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): What's option two?

Six months rather than twelve, with a defined enablement programme, and we agree measurable criteria at the start. If it works, you renew properly in May.
