[10:35] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Which three?
[10:37] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): You'd pick. But I'd want commitment from their managers that they get the time, in writing, because otherwise it's July again.
[10:47] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): That's a reasonable ask.
[10:50] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Third, we fix the estate. Delete the temp workflow, redirect the alerts away from Ravi's mailbox, review the six that are failing and decide for each one whether to fix it or kill it. I'd guess three should be killed.
[11:08] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Probably four.
[11:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Probably four. And fourth — we settle the Guidewire question rather than leaving it hanging, because if claims triage is moving, then the case for this product rests entirely on broker onboarding and you should know that before you renew anything.
[11:29] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): How would we settle it?
[11:32] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Get the claims director in a room with Nadia and have the cross-system conversation. Not with me in the room — this isn't a vendor question.
[11:44] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] That's the right answer and I've been avoiding it.
[11:50] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): We've both been avoiding it.
[11:53] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Because she'll win.
[11:55] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): She might win.
[11:57] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): She'll win on claims and she should. The question is whether she wins on everything.
[12:04] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then that's the meeting to have. And whichever way it goes, you'd know what you're buying.
[12:11] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Can I ask something blunt?
[12:14] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[12:16] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): If we do option two and it doesn't work, do you actually let us leave in May, or does it become a negotiation?
[12:25] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's a six-month term. It ends. There's no auto-renew clause on a term like that and I'd put that in writing.
[12:34] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Because our current contract does auto-renew.
[12:38] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Your current contract auto-renews with sixty days' notice, which means your notice deadline is the thirtieth of September.
[12:47] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] Three weeks.
[12:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Three weeks.
[12:52] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Did you know that, Graham?
[12:54] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): I did not know that.
[12:57] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is why I've said it now rather than on the first of October. I'm not going to auto-renew you into a twelve-month contract you didn't intend to sign.
[13:08] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Some vendors would.
[13:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Some vendors do. It's a terrible way to run a business.
[13:15] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] Right. So I need to serve notice by the thirtieth regardless, to keep my options open.
[13:24] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd suggest you do exactly that. Serve notice, which stops the auto-renew, and then we negotiate the six-month option separately without a clock on it. That's the cleanest thing for you.
[13:39] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): You're telling us to serve notice on our own contract.
[13:44] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'm telling you to preserve your optionality. If you serve notice and then decide to do the six months, that's a new agreement and everyone knows what they're signing.
[13:56] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Ruth, is he allowed to say this?
[13:59] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [laughs] He's said worse.
[14:02] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather have a customer in May than a lawsuit in March.
[14:07] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Nobody's suing anybody.
[14:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No, but you'd be annoyed, and annoyed customers tell other people.
[14:15] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): That's more honest than I expected.
[14:18] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Can I raise the support thing? Since we're being honest.
[14:23] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Please.
[14:25] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): We've raised eleven tickets this year. Four of them we closed ourselves because we'd worked it out before anyone came back.
[14:35] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What was the response time?
[14:38] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Within SLA, technically. But "within SLA" was a message asking us to confirm details we'd already provided in the ticket.
[14:48] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a real complaint and I've heard it before.
[14:52] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): It's not catastrophic. It's just — it's the kind of thing that means I don't raise tickets any more, and then you look at the data and conclude we're happy.
[15:04] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's a very good point and it's slightly chilling.
[15:09] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Low ticket volume can mean two things.
[15:13] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Low ticket volume can mean two things, yes. I'll be more careful with that metric.
[15:19] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): What would you actually change?
[15:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): For the six months, I'd want a fortnightly fifteen-minute call with Nadia. Not a QBR. Fifteen minutes, what's broken, what's annoying, what's stuck. Most of what she's described would have surfaced in the first one.
[15:39] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): I'd do that. Fifteen minutes I can do.
[15:43] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): An hour a month I can't argue with.
[15:46] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Half an hour a month.
[15:48] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Even better.
[15:51] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I put some numbers on option two so you've got something concrete?
[15:56] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Please.
[15:58] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Six months at your current annual rate pro-rata. Four builder seats, unchanged — I'd keep four rather than cut to three, because the whole point is getting more people building. Run tier unchanged, you're nowhere near it. Enablement included, not charged as professional services.
[16:19] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Included?
[16:21] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Included. If I charge you for enablement to fix an adoption problem we partly caused, you'd be right to tell me to go away.
[16:31] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): What's that worth, roughly?
[16:34] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Three properly trained builders is about four days of someone's time. I'd have to check what we'd normally charge.
[16:43] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): We'd normally charge for it. I'd rather not.
[16:47] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): And the criteria? You said measurable criteria.
[16:51] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You'd write them, not me. But if I were you I'd want something like — three people other than Ellie have each built and shipped a production workflow. The failing six are resolved or deleted. The Guidewire question is settled and documented. And broker onboarding cycle time has moved, or you know why it hasn't.
[17:16] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Those are all measurable.
[17:19] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): The Guidewire one isn't a metric.
[17:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No, it's a decision. But it's binary and it's got a date, which is close enough.
[17:29] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): What happens if we hit three of four?
[17:33] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then you decide. I'm not going to pre-commit to a rule about it. If three of four have landed and the fourth is in progress, you'll know whether it's working.
[17:45] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Hm.
[17:47] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Can I add something? The one I'd weight most heavily is the first one. Three people other than Ellie shipping something real. If that happens, everything else is solvable. If it doesn't happen, nothing else matters and you should leave.
[18:05] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): That's a clear statement.
[18:08] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It's the actual test. All the other stuff is symptoms.
[18:13] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Ellie's back in November, incidentally.
[18:17] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's helpful and it's also a trap.
[18:20] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Because she'll just do it all again.
[18:23] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Because she'll do it all again and you'll be back here in a year with a bus factor of one. I'd almost rather do the enablement before she's back.
[18:34] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [pause] That's a good point.
[18:37] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): October, then.
[18:39] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): October would be ideal.
[18:42] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Let me tell you where I am. I'm not going to pretend I'm enthusiastic. If you'd asked me two weeks ago I'd have said we're not renewing.
[18:53] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What's changed?
[18:55] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): You've told me things that aren't in your interest, twice, which makes me trust the rest of it more. And the honest position — that we're paying for Enterprise and getting very little — matches what I'd concluded myself, which is reassuring.
[19:14] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd still say there's a real chance you shouldn't renew.
[19:19] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): I know. That's rather the point.
[19:22] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): My concern is different. I don't think the product is the problem. I think we implemented it badly, one person owned it, and then she left and then the other one went on leave. That's an us problem.
[19:37] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It's partly an us problem. A product that only one person in an organisation can use is a product with an onboarding failure, and that's ours.
[19:49] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): That's generous.
[19:51] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It's not generous, it's true. If we needed Ellie to be exceptional, that's a design problem.
[19:59] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Right. Next steps. What do I need to do by the thirtieth?
[20:05] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Serve notice. It's an email to your account contact, and I'll send you the exact wording and address so it's unambiguous. That stops the auto-renew and costs you nothing.
[20:19] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): And then?
[20:21] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then we have three weeks in October to agree the six-month terms, or you let it lapse on the twenty-ninth of November. Either is a legitimate outcome.
[20:33] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Send me the six-month proposal too, so I can put both in front of finance at the same time.
[20:40] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll send both by Thursday. The proposal, and a one-page comparison of renew-six-months versus lapse, with what you'd lose in each case.
[20:52] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): You'll write the case for lapsing?
[20:55] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll write it accurately. You can decide whether it's compelling.
[21:00] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [laughs] Alright.
[21:03] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): From me — the list of the six failing workflows today, the alert redirection instructions today, and I'll draft what the enablement programme would look like with specific dates rather than a description.
[21:19] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Can you send the export instructions as well?
[21:23] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): For your definitions and run data? Yes.
[21:27] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Regardless of what we decide.
[21:30] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Regardless of what you decide. You should have that anyway and it shouldn't be a leaving-related request.
[21:38] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): And I'll get the meeting with the claims director. I'll do it next week.
[21:44] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's the one that matters most.
[21:47] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): I know. I've known for four months.
[21:51] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Five.
[21:52] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): [crosstalk] Five. Thank you, Nadia.
[21:55] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): [laughs] Sorry.
[21:58] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): One last thing and then I'll let you go. If you do lapse — and I mean this — tell us why properly. Not a form. An actual conversation. Because the Ravi thing and the alerts going to a dead mailbox and nobody noticing a workflow failing for eight months, those are things we should fix for everyone, not just for you.
[22:23] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): I'd do that.
[22:25] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): I'd enjoy that, honestly.
[22:28] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [laughs] I'm sure you would.
[22:31] Graham Attwood (Director of Operations, Pinewood Insurance): Right. Thank you both. That was more useful than I expected and I say that having dreaded it.
[22:39] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks Graham. Thursday for the papers.
[22:43] Nadia Rahman (IT Service Owner, Pinewood Insurance): Bye.
[22:45] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Bye both.

[00:57] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Happy to.
[01:00] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I would also like to move governance earlier. I have to leave at fifty past and governance is my part.
[01:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's do governance and architecture first, current state woven through, and commercials at the end — and if we don't reach commercials, we don't reach commercials.

[01:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That is a comprehensive list.

[02:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No, I didn't take it that way. Jon, take the ones you can answer now and be explicit about the ones you can't.
[02:09] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Right. SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning — both supported, both on Enterprise. Audit logs cover administrative and workflow events. === CALL-005 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-005

STAGE: Evaluation

PARTICIPANTS:

- Nina Patel, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow

TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Morning Noah, morning Hannah. Nina's joining in a couple of minutes, she's coming off another call.
[00:07] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): No problem. Shall I set the frame?
[00:11] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[00:13] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): So you should know we're running this as a bake-off. You and Tray.io. We've had a Tray proof of concept running for about six weeks. This isn't a discovery call for us, we know what we want. This is us testing whether you can do it.
[00:31] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the most useful opening I've had this month. Can I ask what the Tray PoC has shown you?
[00:39] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Connector breadth is genuinely good. No complaints there.
[00:44] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): The engineers hate debugging it.
[00:47] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Hannah's being blunt but she's not wrong. Large visual workflows are hard for our people to reason about. When something goes wrong at step forty of a sixty-step flow, the debugging experience is — it's not good.
[01:04] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a fair criticism of the category, honestly, not just of them. Big visual workflows are hard to debug everywhere. What we'd argue is composition — small subflows rather than one enormous canvas — but I'd rather Nina show you that than me claim it.
[...]
[01:30] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): The other thing you should know is who has to be convinced. I'm the executive sponsor and I'm broadly positive. Hannah and platform engineering score technical fit. Then security, legal, procurement, and the COO approve. So there are a lot of ways for this to die and only one way for it to happen.
[...]
[02:00] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I'm not joking. The main gates are model-risk and auditability. If you can't satisfy those, connector breadth will not save the project. It doesn't matter how many logos are on the integrations page.
[...]
[03:02] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Then you'll know. We have a model risk management framework. Anything that produces an output which influences a decision has to be documented, validated, monitored, and periodically reviewed. If your product puts a language model in a decision path, that model is in scope, and getting something into scope is a nine-month process here.
[...]
[03:39] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then my honest answer is: it depends entirely on how you use it, and you have full control over whether you use it at all. AI steps are explicit, inspectable steps inside a workflow. They're not ambient and they're not in the execution path unless you put them there. Administrators can restrict which models are allowed. Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely.
[04:07] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Can I have a workspace where they're disabled and another where they aren't?
[04:13] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a workspace-level governance question and I believe yes, but I want to confirm the exact granularity rather than guess. I'll come back in writing.
[...]
[04:35] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): My position is that deterministic workflow steps are not a model risk problem and I'd support those tomorrow. Generative steps in a decision path are a nine-month problem. Generative steps that produce a summary a human reads, where the human makes the decision — that's a grey area and I'd want to argue it case by case.
[...]
[05:26] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Grey. A summary for a human reader is defensible. What's not defensible is if that summary silently becomes the input to something automated later.
[05:39] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then the design principle is that the AI output is a leaf node, not an intermediate value. It gets rendered to a person, it doesn't feed the next branch.
[...]
[06:01] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Today it's a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. I'm not going to tell you there's a switch labelled "AI outputs cannot feed decisions", because there isn't.
[...]
[06:24] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Auditability, Hannah.
[06:27] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Right. The list is: SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption details, subprocessor review, EU residency for European records, and contractual language that our data is not used to train shared AI models.
[06:49] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): SOC 2 Type II is the baseline. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Retention configurable within supported ranges. EU data residency available on Enterprise. Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise. And we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[07:17] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): The last one — contractual or marketing?
[07:21] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It needs to be contractual for you to rely on it, and I'd expect legal to insist.
[07:28] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): They will.
[07:30] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): On exportable audit history — define exportable. Because I've had vendors mean "you can download a CSV from a UI" and that is not exportable.
[07:43] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [laughs] API and webhook based, so programmatic. Several customers forward failures and audit events into their own tooling continuously rather than pulling reports. That's the pattern I'd recommend for you.
[07:59] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Into our SIEM.
[08:01] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Into your SIEM, yes.
[08:04] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Then that's satisfactory, subject to seeing the actual payload schema.
[08:10] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'll send the schema.
[08:13] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Good. That's my two gates addressed at the level a call can address them.
[08:20] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Then let's do the use case, because I want Nina to see how ugly it is.
[08:26] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[08:28] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): High-value operational exceptions are currently handled through Slack channels and custom scripts. That's the whole architecture. Someone posts in a channel, someone else picks it up, a script does part of it, and there's a spreadsheet.
[08:46] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And the problem is auditability.
[08:49] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): The problem is auditability and the problem is that four engineers hold the whole thing in their heads. If two of them left in the same quarter we'd be in genuine difficulty.
[09:03] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Three of them are on the same team.
[09:06] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Three of them are on the same team, yes, which is worse.
[09:11] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Do you have telemetry on how often exceptions occur and how long they take?
[09:17] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Partially. We have outcome metrics. Operational telemetry is weak — we can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why, or which dependency failed, or whether the same pattern happened fifteen times last month.
[...]
[10:02] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): The polite version was that our exception handling process was "not evidenced."
[...]
[10:15] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Okay. So let me play back the phase-one candidate as I understood it. Detect failed or delayed partner onboarding events. Enrich them from Salesforce and Snowflake. Open a Jira incident. And maintain a complete audit trail of approvals and remediation steps.
[...]
[11:04] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): So this is run history. Filter by workflow, status, time, or a business field. I'll open a run — and you get every step, its inputs, its outputs, timing, retries, and any human approval with who approved and when.
[...]
[11:28] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [pause] This one. So it timed out on the external call, retried twice, went to the exception queue, a human picked it up, modified a value, approved, and it resumed. And all of that is one record.
[...]
[11:54] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [pause] You can see both here — the value at the point the step ran and the value after the approval form. So yes, but I want to be precise: that's because this approval was configured to collect a structured input. If someone had just clicked approve, there'd be nothing to compare.
[...]
[12:24] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Then design standards matter as much as the platform.
[...]
[12:45] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I flag something? If design standards are load-bearing for your audit position, that should be a pilot deliverable, not an afterthought. As in, the pilot produces a documented standard for how audit-relevant workflows must be built, and that's a deliverable you keep whether or not you buy.
[...]
[13:13] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's write it into the criteria.
[13:17] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Let me show the composition point since it came up at the start. [pause] Rather than one large canvas, you build subflows — partner lookup, enrichment, approval, incident creation — and assemble them. So when something fails, you're debugging a twelve-step subflow, not step forty of sixty.
[13:41] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Can I unit test a subflow?
[13:44] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You can run one in isolation with a given input, yes. Whether that meets your definition of a unit test is a different question, and I suspect it doesn't quite.
[13:57] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It doesn't quite. But running in isolation is most of what I want.
[14:04] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Can I ask what your engineers found hardest in the Tray PoC? Specifically. Because if it's the debugging loop I want to be tested on that, and if it's something else I'd rather know.
[14:19] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It's the debugging loop and it's error handling. Retry semantics were opaque. We couldn't always tell whether something had run twice.
[14:31] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Idempotency.
[14:33] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Idempotency. Yes.
[14:36] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a genuinely hard problem and I'm not going to claim we solve it for you. Each run keeps state, retries are visible in the run record, and you can see whether a step executed. But if a downstream system isn't idempotent and you retry a write, you can absolutely create a duplicate. The mitigation is design — idempotency keys, checks before writes — and it's the same mitigation anywhere.
[...]
[15:24] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Salesforce, Snowflake, Slack, Okta, Jira, and an internal event bus. Required: all of those, plus webhooks and a generic REST connector.
[...]
[15:51] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Not currently.
[15:53] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then that's the one to design for. [16:20] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): That can be arranged.
[16:23] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): What about schema changes? We've had integrations fail because someone renamed a field and nothing surfaced.
[16:31] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): We cache metadata but refresh it, and mapping errors surface on the run. For high-impact flows I'd recommend explicit validation at the start rather than assuming every source field is populated. And you can alert when error rates cross a threshold.
[16:51] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I'd want that tested in the evaluation. With bad data.
[16:56] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Please give us bad data. Genuinely, the pilots that go wrong are the ones run on clean data.
[17:04] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): We have plenty of bad data.
[17:07] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): [crosstalk] We have exceptional bad data.
[17:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs]
[17:12] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): One thing I want to revisit, actually, before we go further.
[...]
[17:19] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I said in the internal session that all approvals have to remain in Jira. I want to soften that. [...]
[18:13] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I make sure I've captured it correctly, though, because it changes scope. Approvals in OrbitFlow are acceptable for low-risk cases subject to audit export quality, with risk tiering to be defined. High-risk approvals remain in Jira.

[18:41] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Environment separation — can we have separate dev and production?

[24:00] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It has a remediation programme, which has a budget, which is a number. Yes.

[24:43] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Engineer hours. That's the four-people problem quantified.
[24:49] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): And adoption. A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation, and our engineers are perfectly capable of routing around things.
[25:02] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): We have a history.
[25:05] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Can I add one? Test the edge cases rather than average time. In your world the average exception is boring and the interesting ten percent is where the audit risk lives.
[25:19] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Yes. Precisely.
[25:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Timing?
[25:24] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Technical bake-off in July. Vendor decision in August. First controlled production workflows in October.
[25:33] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's tight.
[25:35] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): It's tight but it's real. The remediation programme has a date attached to it and that's what's driving the timeline.

[26:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would that satisfy the auditor?
[26:25] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): [pause] No.
[26:28] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Hannah's pause was the answer.
[26:31] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It wouldn't satisfy the auditor. But it would be proposed, and somebody senior would find it attractive, and we'd spend two months on it.
[26:42] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's address it in the pilot criteria explicitly rather than pretending the only alternative is Tray. I'd rather we lose to a documented decision than lose to a two-month detour.
[26:57] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Agreed.

[27:03] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Assuming the security material lines up, I want to move. Send sandbox access and a written proposal for a six-week pilot so we can compare it against Tray properly rather than impressionistically.

[27:23] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): As soon as the sandbox exists and Hannah's had the security pack for long enough to complain about it.
[27:31] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I'll need a week.

[28:15] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Add the note about AI outputs not being enforceable as leaf nodes. I want that written down as a known limitation, not remembered from a call.

[28:34] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And I'd like an hour with whoever owns the event bus, and I'd like bad data.

[29:09] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): You'll have them Friday.

[29:49] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): One correction. It's not a two-horse bake-off, it's a two-horse bake-off where one horse has a six-week head start.

[30:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd much rather know. Right — anything else before we drop?

[30:31] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Three documents, no deck.
[30:34] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Three documents, no deck.

context.text:
=== CALL-009 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-009
DATE: 2026-08-04
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Inkwell Learning
INDUSTRY: Education technology
COMPANY SIZE: 520 employees
STAGE: Solution evaluation
DURATION: 31 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Olivia Grant, SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning
- Darren Wu, Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning
TRANSCRIPT
[00:26] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Yes. So — support volume spikes around school-term launches. Enormously. And the problem isn't the volume itself, we can staff for volume. The problem is that we struggle to distinguish isolated tickets from account-level implementation risk until the escalation reaches an executive.
[...]
[00:53] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): By the time I know, a school district's chief of staff has emailed our CEO. That's the current detection mechanism and it is not a good one.
[...]
[01:07] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Four or five times a term. Which sounds small until you remember each one is a renewal at risk.
[...]
[01:23] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] I am. So — the proposal, as I understand it, is to combine Zendesk ticket patterns, Salesforce account status, and Snowflake product usage to flag accounts needing proactive intervention, and create structured follow-up tasks.
[...]
[01:44] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Right. And my concern is not whether that's technically possible. It obviously is. My concern is data quality. If Salesforce fields are stale, an elegant workflow will still make bad decisions. Beautifully, consistently, at scale.
[02:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a fair challenge and I'd rather have it now.
[02:09] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): There's a specific version of it, actually, and I want to challenge something Olivia said in the last session.
[02:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Here we go.
[02:18] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Olivia talks about account-health scores as though they're reliable. Leadership uses them, they're on the QBR deck, they're in the board pack. But fewer than half our CSMs update the underlying fields consistently. So I would not treat those scores as ground truth, and if we build a workflow that keys off them we've automated a guess.
[02:44] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's — I don't entirely disagree.
[02:49] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): You've disagreed before.
[02:52] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I've disagreed with the framing. I think the scores are directionally useful and you think they're noise.
[03:00] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I think they're noise with a trend in them, which is not the same as useful.
[03:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask a question that might be helpful here?
[03:11] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Please.
[03:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Of the three data sources — Zendesk tickets, Salesforce status, Snowflake usage — which one do you both actually trust?
[03:23] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [immediately] Snowflake.
[03:25] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [crosstalk] Snowflake, yes.
[03:27] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because it's machine-generated. Nobody has to remember to update it.
[03:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And Zendesk?
[03:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Reasonably good. Ticket volume and category are reliable. The sentiment tagging is not, because it's manual.
[03:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And Salesforce.
[03:47] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Salesforce is reliable for the commercial facts — contract dates, ARR, owner. It is unreliable for anything a human has to remember to type.
[04:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's actually a very clean answer and I think it's the design.
[04:06] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Say more.
[04:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Weight the signals by how they're produced. Machine-generated usage data and structured ticket data carry the flag. Human-maintained fields are context you show to the person, not inputs the logic depends on.
[04:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's — yes. That's the right architecture.
[04:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Would that actually have caught the escalations we've had?
[04:37] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's the question, isn't it.
[04:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can you test it? You've got history.
[04:44] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): How would we test it?
[04:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Take the escalations that reached you and run them backwards. For each one, look at what the usage data and ticket data looked like three weeks earlier. If the signal was there, you've got a case. If it wasn't, you've saved yourself a project.
[05:05] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): We could do that with SQL. We don't need a workflow platform to do that.
[05:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You absolutely don't, and you should do it before you buy anything from us.
[05:17] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] Alright. That's not the answer I expected.
[05:22] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): If the signal isn't in the data, we can't manufacture it. And I'd rather you found that out with a query than with a pilot.
[05:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren, could you do that?
[05:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I could do that in a day. Maybe two.
[05:39] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Then why haven't we?
[05:41] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because nobody's asked me to, and because I've been arguing about the health scores instead.
[05:48] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] Fair.
[05:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd suggest making it the first thing, honestly. It's the cheapest way to find out whether this project should exist.
[05:59] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I'm slightly surprised you're saying that.
[06:03] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): If it turns out the signal isn't there, you'd discover it in month three of a pilot and I'd have burned your goodwill and my quarter. I'd rather know in week one.
[06:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Alright. Darren, do it.
[06:19] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I'll do it.
[06:21] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask what you'd look for? Because the answer isn't binary.
[06:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Meaning?
[06:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Meaning it's rarely "the signal was there" or "it wasn't." It's usually "it was there for six of the twelve, and for four of those it was there so early it'd have been indistinguishable from noise."
[06:43] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's a good point. So I'd want the lead time as well as the presence.
[06:50] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And the false positive rate. How many accounts looked the same and turned out fine.
[06:57] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] Yes. That's the harder half.
[07:02] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Why harder?
[07:04] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because to measure false positives I need to know which accounts were fine, and "fine" isn't recorded anywhere. Absence of escalation isn't the same as fine.
[07:17] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): No, it isn't.
[07:20] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): For what it's worth, that's a problem you'd have with any approach, including buying Gainsight properly. It's not an OrbitFlow problem.
[...]
[08:07] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Neither gives us the workflow. Gainsight has the customer success concepts but we haven't implemented them. Looker has the data but no ability to make anything happen. And nothing joins Zendesk to Snowflake to Salesforce in a way that produces an action.
[...]
[09:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll build one that includes them accurately. Whether it's fair is for you to judge, and you should check my numbers.
[...]
[10:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): In this flow — create a structured follow-up task with the account, the signal that triggered it, and links back to the underlying tickets and usage. Assign it to the account's CSM, or to a queue if the owner field is stale. Escalate if nothing happens in N days.
[11:09] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): The escalation. That's the bit I want.
[...]
[11:50] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then route to a group, resolve dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And run history persists so you can see the inputs, which steps ran, and where it stopped.
[...]
[12:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a good question and the honest answer is you need a feedback path or the thing degrades. If a CSM dismisses a flag, that dismissal should be recorded, and you should look at dismissal rates as a health metric for the workflow itself.
[...]
[12:33] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You build it. It's a field on the task and a report. I'm not going to tell you there's a built-in model-monitoring feature, because there isn't.
[...]
[13:01] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the AI use case. As I've got it written: produce a weekly narrative summary of emerging customer themes, with links back to supporting tickets and account records.
[13:14] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Yes. Because I currently get a spreadsheet and I don't read it.
[...]
[14:06] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Can it say "I don't know"? If there isn't a theme this week, will it invent one?
[14:13] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It will if you let it. You can design against that — require a minimum number of supporting tickets before a theme is reported, and route thin cases to review rather than publishing them. What I wouldn't do is rely on the model's own confidence score as a guarantee. The better control is evidence plus workflow policy.
[...]
[14:51] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Can we see the prompt?
[14:53] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. AI steps are explicit, inspectable workflow steps — you can see the prompt, the model, the configuration. Administrators can restrict which models are allowed, and Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely. We log the model configuration used on each run, and we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[15:19] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): That last one matters for us.
[...]
[15:32] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): SSO, audit logs, retention controls, and a clear boundary around student-level data. That last one is the important one.
[...]
[15:47] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): FERPA. We handle data about students in US school districts. Student-level records are subject to specific protections and our position is that they should never leave our warehouse.
[16:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): So the workflow operates on account-level aggregates only.
[16:09] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Correct. Usage counts, engagement rates, ticket volumes at the account level. Never a student record, never a student identifier.
[...]
[17:01] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's an engineering answer that makes the FERPA answer easy. Our counsel would much rather hear "the data never leaves" than "the vendor has controls."
[17:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd note that we should still complete your security review properly. Making the data question moot doesn't remove the vendor assessment.
[...]
[17:29] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): On the rest of your list — SOC 2 Type II baseline, SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise, encryption in transit and at rest, audit logs covering administrative and workflow events, retention configurable within supported ranges. Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, audit export on Enterprise.
[...]
[17:57] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): We are occasionally treated like one by district procurement.
[18:02] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): True. Some districts have their own questionnaire.
[...]
[18:10] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Possibly, for the larger ones. Not for a pilot.
[...]
[18:47] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): The spreadsheet Darren makes. The at-risk review meeting, which is ninety minutes a week of expensive people reading a list. And a chunk of what we're notionally paying Gainsight for.
[...]
[19:07] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I know we're not going to switch it off. I'm saying the spend is questionable.
[...]
[19:36] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Which is why I want the model to be honest. If the answer is "expand Gainsight, it's cheaper", I want to be able to say that.
[...]
[21:02] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Renewal retention. If we intervene three weeks earlier on four accounts a term, and one of them renews that wouldn't have, that pays for it several times over.
[21:16] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's the argument, and it's a good one, but it relies on the counterfactual. We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
[...]
[21:32] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Which is why finance is sceptical of customer success business cases generally.
[21:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is there a leading indicator you could commit to instead? Something measurable that isn't the renewal itself.
[...]
[21:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Time from first signal to first intervention. That's measurable, it's attributable, and it's the thing the system actually changes. Whether earlier intervention improves renewal is a separate hypothesis, and honestly it's one you already believe or you wouldn't have a customer success team.
[...]
[22:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And I'd add — Inkwell wants to measure whether the system identifies at-risk accounts earlier than the current process. That's the actual success criterion and it's testable against history.
[...]
[24:27] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I can have that by the end of next week.
[...]
[24:34] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Then I want to pilot it. And I'll tell you exactly how — we give you twenty historical escalations and we test whether the system would have surfaced them earlier than our current process. Not a demo on clean data. Those twenty, with the data as it actually was.
[...]
[26:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Four or five escalations a term. Fewer than half of CSMs updating fields consistently. Ninety minutes a week on the review meeting. Sixty-two CSMs was firm, the rest were approximate.
[26:59] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): The "fewer than half" is an impression, not a measurement.
[...]
[27:12] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's worth measuring regardless.
[...]
[27:40] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): First — if we do this, the workflow logic has to be in version control somehow. Or at least reviewable. I'm not having business-critical logic that only exists in a web UI.
[27:55] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Version history and change metadata are there, so you can see what changed and when. Definitions can be exported through the API. Whether that satisfies you as version control depends on what you mean — it's not a git integration.
[...]
[28:21] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You can see change metadata and version history in the product. A true side-by-side diff of two workflow definitions — I'd want to confirm what the export gives you rather than promise a diff experience.
[...]
[28:48] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): No. But the last person who owned Gainsight left and that's why we implemented forty percent of it. I want to know that if I get hit by a bus, someone else can pick this up.
[29:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's the right question and it's mostly not a product answer. The product parts are: workflows built as small readable subflows rather than one enormous canvas, version history so someone can see what changed, and run history so someone can see what actually happens. The rest is your operating model — naming conventions, a rule that someone other than the builder can understand each production flow, documentation as a deliverable rather than a hope.
[...]
[29:40] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Largely, yes. What I'd say is that this platform makes it possible. It doesn't make it happen.
[...]
[30:02] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Alright. I'll do the backward analysis and I'll be honest about what it shows. If the signal's not there I'll say so and we'll stop.
[...]
[30:16] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): And if it is there, I'll be more enthusiastic than I've been today.

context.text:
=== CALL-011 (call kind: renewal)
CALL ID: CALL-011
DATE: 2026-09-02
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
CUSTOMER: Lumen Retail Group
INDUSTRY: Grocery retail
COMPANY SIZE: 3,200 employees
STAGE: Renewal / QBR
DURATION: 21 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Fiona Bright, Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group
- Devan Shah, Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Morning both. So this is the quarterly review and it's also the renewal conversation, which I've merged because I didn't think either of you wanted two meetings.
[00:11] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Correct.
[00:13] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): [crosstalk] Very correct.
[00:15] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Maya's here for the commercial part. She'll be quiet until then, allegedly.
[00:21] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Allegedly.
[00:23] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Right. Let me start with numbers and then you tell me what I've missed. You're fourteen months in. Twenty-two workflows in production, up from six at the end of the first quarter. Run volume's roughly two hundred and eighty thousand a month.
[00:41] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): That sounds about right.
[00:43] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Error rate's sitting at one point four percent, which is down from four point one when you started. Most of that improvement came in April.
[00:53] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): April was when we fixed the store-data validation. That was our fault, not yours.
[01:00] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I know, but it counts.
[01:03] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): What I care about is the depot exceptions workflow. Can you give me that one specifically?
[01:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Yes. Median time from exception raised to first action is now forty minutes. It was — Devan, what was it before?
[01:20] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Between two and six hours, depending on who was on.
[...]
[02:16] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Were we charged for those?
[02:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You were charged for two of them. Two were waived — one in March because it was a retry storm caused by a Salesforce outage on their side, and one in May which I waived because you'd flagged it to us proactively before the invoice.
[02:37] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): I didn't know that.
[02:39] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): I knew about March. I didn't know about May.
[02:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): May was a judgement call. I'd rather tell you now than have it look like a discovery in the renewal.
[02:51] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Appreciated. But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
[02:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The run tier is wrong, yes. Which is most of what I want to talk about.
[03:02] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Can I ask something before we get to money?
[03:06] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[03:08] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): The retry storm in March. Has anything changed at your end so that doesn't happen again? Because from our side we did nothing wrong and it cost us twenty thousand runs.
[03:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Partly. There are retry controls and you can set caps per workflow, and we can look at whether yours are configured sensibly — I suspect two or three of them aren't. But if a downstream system is down for six hours and your workflows keep firing, you will burn runs.
[03:43] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): So the answer is configure it better.
[03:47] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): The answer is configure it better, and I should have done that with you in April rather than now. That's on me.
[03:56] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): [pause] Alright.
[03:58] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Can we book that as a session rather than an action item that dies?
[04:04] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Yes. I'll put an hour in with Devan for the fortnight after next.
[04:10] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Fine.

[01:50] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then what are you moving to?
[01:53] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Zapier. Which we had before, which we should probably never have left.
[02:00] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What'll that cost?
[02:02] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need.
[02:08] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So a tenth.
[02:10] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): A tenth, yes.
[02:12] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Will it do everything?
[02:14] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] No. We'll lose the approval steps and we'll lose the run history, which I'll genuinely miss. But nineteen thousand pounds is a member of staff for four months, and when I put it that way to my managing director, the conversation was quite short.
[02:34] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a hard argument to counter.
[02:37] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): It's an impossible argument to counter. And I'd like to say — I did think about it properly. I'm not being flippant. I sat down and listed what we'd lose.
[02:50] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What was on the list?
[02:52] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): The run history. The approval forms, because our contractor sign-off uses those and Zapier can't really do it. And the fact that when something breaks, I know within an hour rather than when a tenant rings up.
[03:09] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Those are the three things that matter.
[03:12] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): They're the three things that matter and they're worth something. They're not worth nineteen thousand pounds a year to a company our size.
[03:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Alastair, do you want to come in?
[03:25] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yeah — Hazel, I mean, I'm sorry it's ended up here. Is there — I mean, is there a version where we look at the pricing? Because I could go and —
[03:37] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Alastair, no. I'm not doing that.
[03:41] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): No, I understand, I just —
[03:44] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): If you can do it for eight thousand now, that tells me you could have done it for eight thousand two years ago, and then I'd be quite cross.
[03:54] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's fair.
[03:57] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Hazel, can I ask about the original purchase?
[04:01] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): You can, and Alastair may not enjoy it.
[04:05] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's fine. Honestly.
[04:08] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): When we bought this, I was told it would scale with us. That we'd start with the fault-reporting workflow and then do compliance, and then service charges, and then contractor management. And that was true — it would have. But we never did any of it.
[04:28] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Why not?
[04:30] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Because we're two hundred and forty people and everyone's already got a job. The roadmap I agreed to in the sales process assumed a version of Oakhill that spent time on process improvement, and we've never once had that time.
[04:47] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Was that discussed?
[04:49] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): It was discussed enthusiastically.
[04:52] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] By whom?
[04:55] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): By both of us, to be fair. I was enthusiastic too. I'm not putting this all on Alastair.
[05:03] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I did — I mean, I remember that conversation and you were quite keen on the compliance one.
[05:11] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I was extremely keen on the compliance one. I've been keen on the compliance one for three years. It has never once reached the top of my list.
[05:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So the purchase was priced against a future that didn't happen.
[05:27] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Yes. That's a good way of putting it. We paid for eleven workflows' worth of value and a plan for forty.
[05:37] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Is there anything we could have done?
[05:40] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] Yes, actually. Two things.
[05:44] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[05:46] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Someone should have noticed after six months that we had four users on a thirty-user plan and said something. Not sold me something. Said something.
[05:58] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a fair criticism. We look at that data.
[06:03] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Do you?
[06:04] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): We look at it. Whether anyone acts on it for an account your size is a different question, and the answer is usually no.
[06:14] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): At least you're honest.
[06:16] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What's the second thing?
[06:19] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): There should be a smaller plan. Something for a company that needs five workflows and three users and doesn't need thirty seats. If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer and I'd probably have done the compliance one eventually.
[06:39] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): There isn't one.
[06:41] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I know there isn't. Alastair told me at the time.
[06:45] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I did say that.
[06:47] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): You did say that, in fairness. You said the entry point is Growth and that's the entry point.
[06:54] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Did you consider not buying?
[06:57] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I did. And I decided the fault-reporting problem was bad enough to justify it, which it was. For about a year.
[07:07] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What changed after a year?
[07:10] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Nothing changed. That's the thing. It kept working. But the pain it solved stopped being fresh, and the invoice kept arriving, and eventually somebody looks at a renewal and asks what this is for.
[07:26] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): The problem being solved becomes invisible.
[07:30] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): The problem being solved becomes invisible. Exactly that. Nobody remembers how bad it was.
[07:38] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Do you think you'll regret it?
[07:41] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] Possibly. I think there'll be a moment in about four months when something breaks and nobody notices for two days and I'll think, well, that used to be handled.
[07:55] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): And then?
[07:57] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): And then I'll deal with it, because that's a two-day problem and not a nineteen-thousand-pound problem.
[08:04] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a rational position.
[08:07] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I've had a lot of time to think about it. I've been putting off this decision since May.
[08:14] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Can I ask about the last year of service? How was it?
[08:19] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Fine. Genuinely fine. I think I've raised two tickets in two years and both were answered.
[08:27] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Did anyone from us contact you?
[08:30] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): You did, in — March? An email about a new feature.
[08:36] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): A product announcement.
[08:38] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): A product announcement, yes.
[08:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's not contact.
[08:43] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): No, it isn't.
[08:45] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] I'm going to be direct with you. Your account was in a segment that doesn't get an assigned CSM. I'm on this call because it's a churn, not because I've been managing you.
[08:59] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I'd worked that out. You've been very good today but you clearly hadn't heard of us before Tuesday.
[09:07] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Monday, actually.
[09:09] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [laughs] Monday.
[09:12] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'm not going to pretend otherwise.
[09:15] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I don't mind. It's a commercial reality. But it does rather answer the question of why nobody noticed the four users.
[09:25] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It does.
[09:27] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I say something?
[09:29] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Go on.
[09:31] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I think — looking back, I probably should have pushed harder on whether you had the capacity for the roadmap we talked about. I was excited about it and you were excited about it and neither of us asked who was actually going to do it.
[09:49] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] That's a good thing to say.
[09:53] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've been thinking about it since Ruth sent me the notice.
[09:58] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): For what it's worth, Alastair, I don't think you did anything wrong. You sold me a good product that does what it says. I just bought more of it than I needed.
[10:10] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks. I appreciate that.
[10:13] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Practical things. What do you need for the exit?
[10:18] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Our workflow definitions, if only so I know how to rebuild them in Zapier.
[10:24] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): You can export those through the API. I'll send instructions — and honestly, for eleven simple workflows, screenshots might be more useful than the JSON.
[10:36] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Screenshots would be much more useful.
[10:39] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then I'll get someone to produce those. It's not a thing we offer, but it's eleven workflows and it'll take an hour.
[10:48] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): That's kind.
[10:50] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What about run history?
[10:52] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Do I need it?
[10:54] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): You tell me. Is there any compliance reason you'd need to show what happened to a fault report from eighteen months ago?
[11:03] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] Possibly, actually. There's a Building Safety Act angle on fault response times.
[11:11] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then take the export. It's better to have it and not need it.
[11:16] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): How do I get it?
[11:18] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Run events API. I'll send the pagination details, because two years of records will hit a limit and you'll assume it's broken.
[11:28] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): I definitely would have assumed that.
[11:31] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Everyone does. And I'll arrange a deletion confirmation for afterwards with an actual date on it.
[11:39] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Thank you.
[11:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Your contract ends the eleventh of November. Do you want read-only access past that?
[11:47] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Two weeks would help. We'll be running both in parallel through October.
[11:53] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'll give you until the end of November. No charge.
[11:58] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): That's generous.
[12:00] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It's not generous, it's just not petty.
[12:03] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [laughs] Some vendors are petty.
[12:07] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Some vendors are very petty.
[12:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): One last question. If we did have a smaller plan — five hundred a month, five workflows, three users, no approval forms — would you buy it?
[12:22] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [pause] With the approval forms, yes. Without them, no, because that's the bit Zapier can't do and it's the only thing I'll actually miss.
[12:34] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So approval forms are the feature.
[12:37] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): For a company like us, the approval forms and the run history are the whole product. The rest is capability I'll never reach.
[12:47] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's genuinely useful and I'll pass it on.
[12:51] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Will anything happen?
[12:53] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Probably not. But it'll be one more data point and eventually someone counts them.
[13:00] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [laughs] That's the most realistic thing anyone's said to me all week.
[13:06] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Thank you, Hazel. Genuinely.
[13:09] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): Thanks both. Alastair — no hard feelings.
[13:14] Alastair McCrae (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): None at all. Good luck with the compliance one.
[13:18] Hazel Wren (Operations Director, Oakhill Property): [laughs] It'll never happen. Bye.

answer.summary:
Across these two churn post-mortems, the departing customers said OrbitFlow could have been more realistic about implementation and fit: in both calls, they wanted OrbitFlow to ask who would actually build the workflows and whether the customer had capacity for the roadmap. They also said OrbitFlow should have surfaced the right level of help earlier — not just onboarding or an unanswered template question, but hands-on assistance / services for the first real workflows — and, for smaller customers, offered a smaller cheaper plan or otherwise priced the product around actual usage. 

The common theme is not that the product failed to work; it’s that OrbitFlow sold an ambition the customer couldn’t sustain, and in one case missed that the key features were approval forms and run history rather than the whole broader platform.

context.text:
=== CALL-014 (call kind: churn)
CALL ID: CALL-014
DATE: 2026-09-18
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
CUSTOMER: Verity Payments
INDUSTRY: Payments
COMPANY SIZE: 800 employees
STAGE: Churn post-mortem
DURATION: 21 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Kwame Boateng, Head of Operations, Verity Payments
- Sarah Lindqvist, Engineering Manager, Verity Payments
TRANSCRIPT
[01:21] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a month after I took the account.
[01:24] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): It's not about you. I want to be clear about that.
[01:29] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'd still like to know what happened in February.
[01:33] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): February was when we tried to build the settlement reconciliation workflow and couldn't.
[01:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Couldn't, or found it hard?
[01:43] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Couldn't, in the sense that the effort exceeded the value by a factor I couldn't justify to my team.
[01:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Tell me about it specifically.
[01:54] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Our settlement provider is a mid-sized European processor. You don't have a connector for them. Nobody does, to be fair — Workato doesn't either.
[02:06] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So what was the difference?
[02:09] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): The difference is that we ended up writing a custom integration either way, and once you've accepted you're writing custom integrations, you start asking what the platform is actually giving you.
[02:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And what was the answer?
[02:26] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Orchestration and run history, which are genuinely good. But not enough on their own for what we were paying.
[02:35] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): And this is where I'd push back on Sarah slightly.
[02:39] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Go on.
[02:41] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.
[...]
[05:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] It's a paid professional services engagement.
[...]
[05:30] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is possibly the problem. If the thing that makes the product succeed is a paid add-on, and the customer doesn't know they need it until it's too late —
[05:41] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Then you've designed a product that fails by default for people like me.
[...]
[05:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[06:00] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): My team quite liked it. The run history is genuinely better than what we'd have built. The exception queues are good. When something failed at three in the morning, we could see why, and that's not nothing.
[06:16] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So why did you support leaving?
[06:19] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations. And because the licence cost was being justified by a benefit — business-user autonomy — that wasn't materialising.
[06:39] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Say the other thing.

[20:36] Ava Sinclair (Staff Software Engineer, Juniper Cloud Tools): They're very much not the same thing.
[20:39] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): No. So: manual re-trigger yes, deterministic replay no.

[20:52] Ava Sinclair (Staff Software Engineer, Juniper Cloud Tools): [pause] If the exported definitions turn out to be unreadable. If subflows are billed individually and the economics invert. And if the Postgres connector does something stupid.
[21:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Those are three testable things and two of them I can answer in writing this week.
[21:14] Ava Sinclair (Staff Software Engineer, Juniper Cloud Tools): Then answer them in writing this week.
[21:17] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I will.

[21:26] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
